items.title: 52300_Trummy Young oral history interview
items.q: He used Buck as the leader on quite a few things, and I played a few of those things with Buck

ctx.x: Also did a record date -- and I forgot the tune we did on it with Tony Scott, the clarinet player, and Sarah Vaughan was singing on this date. I don't know if we did "Chelsea Bridge." Ben Webster was on it also. But we did some good things. It's been so long, I forgot the particular tunes that we did on this thing. They were good.

And, of course, John Hammond used to have a lot of dates around there then because he used to use Buck Clayton on quite a few. He used Buck as the leader on quite a few things, and I played a few of those things with Buck, and they would really swing, you know, some of these things.

But almost every day you'd be recording with somebody. I know Eckstein came in town. He wanted to record, and he used a big band, with Eckstein -- a lot of us that never really played with him, we recorded with his band around, Dexter Gordon, myself, a bunch of us did.

items.title: 67246_Buck Clayton oral history interview
items.q: He added on the Illinois Jacquet. He added on Rex Stewart, Trummy Young, Roy Eldridge, Coleman.

ctx.x: Willie Smith. So the first one to be cross-Country was only three horns. That was Lester and Coleman Hawkins and myself and Helen

Humes, Kenny Kersey on piano. And we came all the way from Los Angeles to New York. That was the end of it. Then later, he started adding on. He added on the Illinois Jacquet. He added on Rex Stewart, Trummy Young, Roy Eldridge, Coleman. And it ended up being a great big show. But at least we made the first cross, cross Country one.
When I first heard you after the War it seemed to me that you were playing with much more power and range than you did before the War.
